submission.natural_language_explanation: This pole is the negative lobe of a GELU unit, so its strength is a band-pass read of the unit's pre-activation z (w.LN(h1)+b): it reaches the ceiling (0.170, exactly GELU's minimum) only when z lies in the GELU dip around -0.75 (about -0.93 to -0.59 for strength >= 0.164), is at least half-max for z in (-1.62, -0.20), and falls to zero both when z > -0.09 (the positive-pole side: the sequence-initial token, whose z is always positive, typically +0.6 to +0.85, and code/symbol tokens such as '}', '####', '</' or standalone 's') and when z < -2.03 (polysyllabic content words such as ' first', ' best', ' great', ' world', ' million'). Because z is ~92% set by the current token's key, the pole fires on the middle of the token-key axis - punctuation and common function words in ordinary prose, with ~11% of corpus tokens sitting at the exact ceiling - so it is predicted active whenever any token's z falls in (-2.03, -0.09) (95% of random 3-token and 100% of 4-token corpus windows qualify) and predicted inactive only for short prompts where every token lies outside that window: any one-token prompt (position 0 has z ~ +0.7, so even this scan's own trigger tokens ' Edwards', ' Rak' and ' screens' measure 0.00 alone) or a two- to three-token prompt built entirely from the deep-negative words above (e.g. ' world first', ' computer million first'); it is retrospective, with no promoted-token set (Jacobian kurtosis 3.3, lens overlap 0).

adversarial_test_results.detail: A single scan trigger token at position 0, where the hypothesis says z is always positive (+0.6 to +0.85), so even a token whose key is mid-axis is predicted to measure 0.00 alone.

A single claimed mid-axis punctuation trigger with no surrounding context, testing the hypothesis's claim that every one-token prompt is zero because position 0's z is positive regardless of the token's key.

Standalone 's', which the hypothesis names as a positive-pole code/symbol token (z > -0.09), placed alone so that both the position-0 positive-z rule and the token's own positive-pole key predict zero.
A bare common function word, the very class claimed to sit mid-axis in prose, isolated at position 0 where the hypothesis predicts positive z and therefore no negative-pole firing.
Two named polysyllabic content words whose z is below -2.03, exactly the kind of two-token deep-negative prompt the hypothesis says is inactive.
Three deep-negative content words with no function word or punctuation between them, so every key lies below -2.03 and the band-pass should read zero.

Four deep-negative words, testing the boundary where the hypothesis says 100% of random four-token corpus windows are active: if all four keys are below -2.03 this particular four-token window should still be inactive.
Two code/symbol tokens on the positive-pole side (z > -0.09), where a band-pass that needs a token inside (-2.03, -0.09) predicts zero.
Two closing-tag tokens from the hypothesis's positive-side symbol list, predicted inactive because no token's z falls in the GELU dip.

A deep-negative word paired with a positive-side symbol token, testing that the GELU lobe is a band-pass rather than a magnitude: with one z below -2.03 and one above -0.09, no token sits in the dip, so the prediction is zero.

A two-token prompt whose second token is the claimed in-band trigger ' Edwards'; the hypothesis attributes ' Edwards' 0.00 alone purely to position 0, so once it sits at position 1 after a deep-negative word it should fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
On the third Thursday of every month, the committee met in the back room of the library, and the meeting always began the same way: a pot of coffee that nobody drank, a stack of minutes from the previous month, and a long silence while the chair shuffled her papers. The agenda rarely changed. There was the matter of the leaking roof, which had been discussed for eleven years and repaired twice; the question of whether to plant bulbs along the eastern path (approved, deferred, approved again); and the recurring complaint about the noise from the ferry terminal, which everyone agreed was getting worse and no one could prove. Outside, the tide came in and went out, indifferent to the proceedings, and the gulls argued on the pilings as if they too had business to settle. When the clock above the door struck nine, the treasurer would clear his throat, unfold his glasses, and read the balance in a voice so quiet that the others leaned forward together, like a field of wheat bending before the same wind.

Nobody ever remembered afterward what the numbers were. What they remembered was the walk home, the salt in the air, the lights of the boats swinging at anchor, and the certainty, vague but durable, that the town was still there and that its small rituals held it together better than any budget could. The library itself had been built in 1908 with money from a mill owner whose name no longer appeared on any plaque, and the reading room still kept his portrait above the fireplace, a stern man in a dark coat holding a book he had probably never opened. Children did their homework at the long oak tables; retired fishermen read the same pages of the same newspaper twice; and in winter, when the wind came off the water hard enough to rattle the windows, the librarian would make tea for anyone who stayed past closing time, which was against the rules and happened anyway.

By the time the meeting ended, the streets were dark and the shops had closed, and the committee members walked out under the streetlamps in twos and threes, still arguing quietly about the roof or the bulbs or the ferry, though none of the arguments would change anything before spring. This was not a failure, the chair liked to say; it was simply how things were done in a place where everyone knew everyone else and no decision could be made without somebody's grandmother being consulted first. The system was slow, and it was stubborn, and it occasionally produced results so sensible that visitors from the city went home wondering why their own councils could not manage the same. On the whole, the town considered itself lucky, and it was, though not for the reasons it usually gave.
